parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what causes pressure when you push on a surface - which two quantities matter, how hard you push and how large the surface is, and in which direction the push must act to count?
parts.proper_answer: Pressure is the normal force per unit cross-sectional area, $p = F/A$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What pressure really means**
Imagine pushing with your hand on a table. The effect you feel spread out depends not just on how hard you push, but over how big an area that push is spread. That is why a sharp pin hurts more than a flat hand for the same push.

Step 2: **Writing the definition precisely**
Only the component of force perpendicular to the surface counts, called the normal force. So in symbols: $$p = \frac{F}{A}$$ where $F$ is the normal force in $\text{N}$ and $A$ is the area in $\text{m}^2$.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Explain how hydrostatic pressure results in an upthrust force acting on a solid object immersed in a liquid.

markscheme_points.text: (due to difference in depth there is a) difference in pressure between top and bottom (of ball)
(due to pressure difference, upwards) force on bottom of ball is greater (than downwards force on top of ball, so resultant force is upwards)

hints: Hint 1: Picture the top and bottom of the ball at different depths in the liquid - how does liquid pressure change with depth, $p = h\rho g$?
Hint 2: Now compare the push of the liquid on the top face with the push on the bottom face - which is larger and what is the direction of the net result?
parts.proper_answer: Pressure in the liquid increases with depth, so pressure on the bottom of the object is greater than on the top. Hence the upward force on the bottom is greater than the downward force on the top, giving a resultant upward force called upthrust.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Pressure grows with depth**
In a liquid, the deeper you go the more liquid is above you weighing down. So hydrostatic pressure follows $$p = h\rho g$$ The bottom of the ball is deeper than the top, so $p_{bottom} > p_{top}$.

Step 2: **From pressure difference to net force**
Pressure means the liquid pushes on each surface with force $F = pA$. The top feels a downward push $F_{top} = p_{top}A$ and the bottom feels an upward push $F_{bottom} = p_{bottom}A$. Since $p_{bottom} > p_{top}$, the upward push wins. That net upward force is the upthrust.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
A small steel ball of radius $r$ and mass $m$ falls vertically at terminal speed $v$ through oil.

The viscous drag force $D$ that acts on the ball is given by

$$D = 6\pi\eta r v$$

where $\eta$ is a property of the oil called its viscosity.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking of the one force that always acts on any mass near Earth, even without any liquid - which way does it point?
Hint 2: Now add the two effects of the oil - one is the buoyancy push you met in (a)(ii), the other is the friction-like resistance that opposes motion through a viscous fluid.
Hint 3: Check directions for a ball moving downwards - which forces try to hold it up and which pulls it down, and remember all arrows must start from the ball?
parts.proper_answer: One arrow vertically downwards from ball labelled weight. Two arrows vertically upwards from ball, one labelled upthrust and one labelled (viscous) drag.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Weight pulls down**
Every mass has weight $W = mg$ pulling it toward the centre of the Earth. So draw one arrow starting at the ball pointing straight down and label it weight.

Step 2: **Oil pushes up twice**
The oil gives an upthrust due to displaced liquid, acting upwards whether the ball moves or not. It also gives viscous drag $D = 6\pi\eta r v$ which always opposes motion. Since the ball falls down, drag acts up.

Step 3: **Completing the free-body diagram**
You should have three arrows all starting from the ball: one long arrow down for weight, and two arrows up, one labelled upthrust and one labelled drag or viscous drag. At terminal speed the two upward arrows together balance the downward arrow.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the SI base units of $\eta$.

markscheme_points.text: SI base units of D: kg m s^-2
base units of η: kg m s^-2 / (m × m s^-1) = kg m^-1 s^-1

hints: Hint 1: Rearrange $D = 6\pi\eta r v$ to make $\eta$ the subject and remember $6\pi$ has no units - what combination of $D$, $r$ and $v$ gives $\eta$?
Hint 2: Write the base units for force $D$ as $\text{kg m s}^{-2}$, for radius $r$ as $\text{m}$ and for speed $v$ as $\text{m s}^{-1}$, then combine them to simplify.
parts.proper_answer: $\eta = D/(6\pi r v)$ so base units are $\text{kg m s}^{-2}/(\text{m} \times \text{m s}^{-1}) = \text{kg m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Isolate viscosity**
$6\pi$ is just a number, so units of $\eta$ come from the rest of the equation. Rearranging: $$D = 6\pi\eta r v$$ $$\eta = \frac{D}{6\pi r v}$$ So units of $\eta$ = units of $D$ divided by (units of $r$ times units of $v$).

Step 2: **Insert base units**
Force $D$ has base units of $\text{kg m s}^{-2}$ from $F = ma$. Radius $r$ is $\text{m}$. Speed $v$ is $\text{m s}^{-1}$. Hence: $$\text{units of } \eta = \frac{\text{kg m s}^{-2}}{\text{m} \times \text{m s}^{-1}} = \text{kg m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$$

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem:
The oil in (b) has a density of $920\text{ kg m}^{-3}$ and a viscosity of $4.7$ in SI units.

The steel ball has a mass of $2.4 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg}$ and a radius of $4.2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: Show that the upthrust force acting on the ball is $2.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ N}$.
hints: Hint 1: Recall upthrust equals the weight of oil displaced by the ball - how can you get that displaced mass from oil density and the volume of a sphere of radius $r$?
parts.proper_answer: Upthrust $= \rho V g = \rho (4/3)\pi r^3 g = 920 \times (4/3)\pi \times (4.2 \times 10^{-3})^3 \times 9.81 = 2.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ N}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Upthrust is weight of displaced oil**
Archimedes tells us upthrust = weight of fluid pushed aside. That is mass of displaced oil times $g$, and mass = density times volume: $$U = \rho V g$$

Step 2: **Put in the sphere volume**
For a sphere $$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$$ So: $$U = 920 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi \times (4.2 \times 10^{-3})^3 \times 9.81$$ $$U \approx 2.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ N}$$ This matches the value to show.

enrichment.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Recall upthrust equals the weight of oil displaced by the ball - how can you get that displaced mass from oil density and the volume of a sphere of radius $r$?

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the terminal speed $v$ of the ball.
hints: Hint 1: At terminal speed acceleration is zero, so forces balance - how are weight downwards and the two upward forces in (b)(i) related?
Hint 2: Write out each term with numbers: $mg$ for weight, $2.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ N}$ for upthrust, and $6\pi\eta r v$ for drag, leaving $v$ as the only unknown.
Hint 3: Rearrange to $v = (mg - U)/(6\pi\eta r)$ and check your powers of ten carefully before calculating.
parts.proper_answer: At terminal speed $mg = U + 6\pi\eta r v$, giving $v = 0.056\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use zero net force at terminal speed**
Terminal means constant velocity, so resultant force is zero. Downward must equal upward: $$\text{weight} = \text{upthrust} + \text{drag}$$ $$mg = U + 6\pi\eta r v$$

Step 2: **Substitute the data**
Weight is: $$mg = 2.4 \times 10^{-3} \times 9.81$$ So the equation becomes: $$(2.4 \times 10^{-3} \times 9.81) = 2.8 \times 10^{-3} + 6\pi \times 4.7 \times 4.2 \times 10^{-3} \times v$$

Step 3: **Solve for v**
Rearrange: $$v = \frac{mg - U}{6\pi\eta r}$$ $$v = \frac{2.354 \times 10^{-2} - 0.28 \times 10^{-2}}{6\pi \times 4.7 \times 4.2 \times 10^{-3}}$$ $$v \approx 0.056\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ downwards. The small value makes sense in very viscous oil.
